sources.headline: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?
sources.text: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Starlink terminals, which connect to thousands of SpaceX satellites in obit, are often camouflaged on the battlefieldByTom McArthur and Tiffany WertheimerUpdated 15 October 2026 12:25 BSTStarlink satellites operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX provide high-speed internet - something modern war relies heavily on.For Ukraine, it is vital for communications on the battlefield and effective drone warfare.Using Starlink, Ukrainian drones can stay connected to operators over longer distances than conventional radio networks and are less vulnerable to jamming.But on Tuesday night, Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection. This disrupted some battlefield "missions", a top Ukrainian official said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks.The restriction at 100mph (160km/h) meant that any drone travelling faster than that lost connection and was effectively useless. "Starlink gives Ukraine the ability to see what's coming, to protect people," Kurt Volker, former US ambassador to Nato, told the BBC's Radio 4 Today programme. "If you cut that off, then more people are going to get killed - and that is a very cynical and callous decision to slow that down the way that has been done."Connectivity had been restored by Wednesday evening.The move has once again shown how Starlink can impact the conflict, which has been raging since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Operators use the Starlink network to stay connected to weapons like drones, so they can see targets in real timeWhat are Starlink and Starshield?Starlink is an internet network that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and battlefields. It currently relies on more than 10,000 active satellites, making Starlink the world's largest satellite constellation.It is owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, and is the company's biggest revenue driver.While Starlink is for civilian use, Starshield is its military-grade sister service, designed for the Pentagon. Starshield relies on the Starlink network, but has greater security like enhanced encryption so that sensitive information can be transmitted without interception.The US government has allowed Ukraine to use Starlink and Starshield in its defence against Russia. Musk cut Moscow's access to the service in February, giving Kyiv an advantage in the conflict.How does Starlink work on a battlefield?Put simply, Starlink uses its thousands of satellites to ping high-speed internet back to almost every corner of the globe, using terminals on the ground that users can easily buy and set up themselves. As Musk said, they have two instructions: "point at sky, plug in".This makes them ideal for use on the battlefield."It's a connection… that you can basically use pretty fast, you don't need any special equipment, you don't need to prepare, you just go to the field and usually it works," Neo, a soldier with one of Ukraine's drone reconnaissance units, told the Today programme."It simplifies our work because we can translate or stream our reconnaissance operations," he added.The network has become "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", George Barros from the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air forces.In Ukraine, both Starlink (the civilian service) and Starshield (the military service) are used, depending on what communications are needed.It is crucial for the effective use of weapons such as drones, which connect to the network so that operators can see their targets in real time, effectively minimising the time between "sensor-to shooter", Barros told the BBC.Because Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, when Ukraine sends long-range missiles deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.When it comes to Ukraine's self-defence, it relies on the Starlink network to protect its own skies against incoming Russian attacks, especially jet-powered Shahed drones, Barros added.Shaheds fly at speeds in excess of 198mph (319 km/h), meaning the Starlink restriction made Ukrainian efforts to chase them down all but impossible.For Neo, this means that any deliberate restrictions on the Starlink network are "a betrayal".With no ready replacement for the Starlink network, any speed restrictions or loss of connectivity have major implications for Ukraine defences, and the recent limits have shown how dependent Kyiv is on the network.Image source, Lev Radin/ Getty ImagesImage caption, Starlink terminals, like this one in Ukraine's Donetsk region, are quick and easy to set up, making them ideal for use on the battlefieldWhile Starlink can provide access nearly everywhere in the world, that does not mean it can be accessed everywhere, and countries must be licenced to use it.Russia is one place where it is not authorised, although Kyiv has in the past said that Moscow was still getting hold of the terminals and using them in occupied territory in Ukraine."If SpaceX obtains knowledge that Starlink terminal is being used by a sanctioned or unauthorized party, we investigate the claim and take actions to deactivate the terminal if confirmed," Starlink said in 2024.But with tens of thousands of terminals in Ukraine alone, it could be a near impossible task to determine which terminals are authorised and which ones are not.Why did Starlink restrict drone speeds?The answer remains unclear. During a visit to London on Wednesday, Zelensky had said he hoped it was just a mistake, however, in a later interview with the Financial Times, he said: "It was not a technical problem, it was the will."Musk said that Starshield is managed by the US government and suggested the Pentagon could be responsible."Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," he wrote on X, external. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS [the president of the United States]."He added: "Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."The BBC has contacted the White House and Pentagon for comment.Image source, EPAImage caption, A Ukrainian soldier attaches a Starlink transmitter to a 'Vampire' attack drone in the Donetsk region, eastern Ukraine, in JuneThe restrictions on Tuesday night came as Russia launched deadly attacks against Ukraine that left 600,000 without power and hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military. Residents said they received no warning of incoming drones before they hit."It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Zelensky's adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram on Wednesday morning.Relations between the US and Ukraine have worsened recently, especially since the US announced a deal with Russia to import its diesel into the American market.Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin, and in response Donald Trump said he thinks "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president".On Sunday, Trump announced a ceasefire on energy infrastructure, but three days later, Ukraine said it would resume the strikes, accusing Russia of ignoring it (the Kremlin said it had never agreed to a ceasefire), and the US of withdrawing crucial support.Zelensky has accused the US of threatening to withhold intelligence if Ukraine continues striking Russian oil facilities. Trump has denied this, but last week told reporters that Zelensky had "better damn well stop" the strikes.While in London, Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US.Trump's deal with Russia is his administration's latest effort to lower US fuel prices ahead of next month's midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war. That conflict, which started in February, has seen prices skyrocket, souring his standing with the American public.

sources.headline: Wes Streeting urges US to back Ukraine on Washington visit after Starlink row
sources.text: Wes Streeting urged the US to stand by Ukraine on his visit to the American capital and sought to cool tensions between the two countries in the wake of the Starlink row that is threatening to set back Kyiv’s war effort.The British defence secretary, giving a speech before a meeting with his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, argued that supporting Ukraine was in the long-term interests of Washington, and a business opportunity.Taking questions after his address, Streeting acknowledged “the challenges of recent days”, a reference to the row over the sudden decision of the US government on Monday to limit the use of Starlink by Ukraine’s military.He said it was “a reminder of two things – one is that American support in Ukraine has been significant and it has made, I think, a real impact in the Ukrainian war effort. And we and the Ukrainians would feel the absence of that.”The second was that there was “an enormous opportunity for the US in terms of the support for Ukraine”, a reference to the future “defence-industrial relationship” between the countries.Streeting was speaking at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a US thinktank, before a potentially difficult meeting with Hegseth amid tensions over Ukraine, Iran and the Middle East.The two men were also expected to discuss the safety of US military bases in the UK, after an Iranian threat prompted the US to withdraw B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, and whether the two countries would come together to help Saudi Arabia, which has come under attack from Yemen’s Houthis.Streeting and Hegseth during a meeting at the Pentagon. Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersBut it is Ukraine that is the most urgent issue. A day ago, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he felt personally betrayed by Donald Trump after the US government appeared to have throttled a version of the Starlink satellite internet service used by Ukraine’s military.Ukrainian officials have reported that the US has also threatened to cut the sharing of intelligence used by Ukraine to detect incoming missiles if it does not abandon its attacks on refineries, aimed at hurting the Russian economy.The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, meeting Zelenskyy in London on Wednesday, said the UK would stand by Ukraine.Streeting said: “There’s rarely been a more important time for Britain and America to come together.”Developing the theme, he made a direct appeal to the US audience. “The people of Ukraine are fighting for a principle that runs through the finest traditions of American political thought,” he said, which was “that a free people have a right to determine their own destiny”.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotionTrump has vacillated over supporting Ukraine against Russia since returning to the White House, while support among US Republicans for Kyiv has been mixed. But Streeting argued that helping Ukraine was also a matter of national self-interest for the US as well as the UK.“Ukraine may be thousands of miles from American shores, but if aggression is rewarded, if borders can be redrawn by force, if the sovereignty of nations becomes negotiable, the consequences will not remain confined to Ukraine or to my continent,” he said.The change to Starlink happened without warning at about 1am, when Ukrainian soldiers reported that terminals on drones were no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph, rendering communications inoperable.It led to a dramatic halt to mid-strike drone attacks on targets in Russian occupied territories on the frontline, and concerns about Ukraine’s ability to intercept new Russian jet-powered attack craft that are bombing its cities.Trump has been trying to put pressure on Ukraine to halt its bombing of Russian oil refineries in a desperate attempt to reduce world oil prices before the US midterm elections. He agreed to buy diesel from Russia earlier this month.

Can a flick of a switch really be enough for Donald Trump and Elon Musk to end Ukraine's hopes of holding out against Russia? With Kyiv already reeling from daily strikes by Russia's new motor-powered drones, the United States decision to slow SpaceX Starlink service felt immediately Wednesday when air raid warnings failed.

We'll check the status on Starlink - reportedly back up to speed, ask if Volodymyr Zelenskiy has any friends in Washington that can convince an administration that prefers diesel deals with Moscow to supporting Ukraine, and whether supporters of Kyiv have run out of road. They're striving to weene themselves off eight decades of depending on Washington for their defense. Do they have any agency? If not, is it the end of Ukraine, the end of Nato... and even the European Union as we know it?

sources.headline: Ukraine says its Starshield access is back
sources.text:
Ukraine says its access to SpaceX's Starshield has been restored. It's the system the country uses for its offensive drone attacks on Russia.
Transcript
STEVE INSKEEP, HOST: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he's going back to attacking Russian oil refineries, which is something President Trump asked him not to do. Zelenskyy told the Financial Times today that he held off for a few days, but not anymore.MICHEL MARTIN, HOST: It's the latest sign of a division between Trump and Ukraine. Another sign is in the skies over Ukraine. The satellite communications system the U.S. gives Ukraine suddenly, but briefly, faced crippling restrictions. In a few minutes, we'll ask Representative Mike Quigley, co-chair of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus, for his take on what's going on there, but we're going to start with the details.INSKEEP: NPR's Greg Myre is following this. Greg, good morning.GREG MYRE, BYLINE: Hi, Steve.INSKEEP: OK. Was the United States trying to limit Ukraine's ability to fight?MYRE: Steve, no one is saying this explicitly, but given the evidence we have, that certainly seems to be the case, and we do have a new development this morning. Ukraine's defense ministry is saying that this satellite network is back and working as normal. And by way of explanation, many people know the satellite communication system Starlink. This is part of Elon Musk's empire. But there's also a military version called Starshield that he built for the U.S. government and military. The Pentagon shares this with Ukraine, which uses it to guide its drones, but yesterday Ukraine discovered quite abruptly that the Starshield system had suddenly been greatly restricted.INSKEEP: In what way?MYRE: Ukraine said that when its drones exceed 100 miles per hour, which is absolutely routine...INSKEEP: Sure.MYRE: ...The communication was automatically cut between the drone and the drone operator, and this effectively made the aircraft useless. Ukraine depends on this Starshield system for both its offensive drones that attack Russia and defensive drones to protect against Russian airstrikes. And so Ukraine said it was trying to figure that out, but it seems it may have now been resolved.INSKEEP: OK. So you said nobody's explaining this explicitly, but are SpaceX or the Trump administration saying anything?MYRE: Yeah. Elon Musk went on X and said Starshield is, quote, "controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately," he said, the president. Now, the White House and the Pentagon have not commented directly on this. But again, according to Musk, if there were something going on, that would be because the White House and/or the Pentagon had done something.INSKEEP: OK. So is there some connection between these two events, the sudden Starshield outage and the disagreement between Trump and Ukraine over whether Ukraine should be attacking Russian oil facilities?MYRE: Well, Steve, NPR's Ukraine correspondent Joanna Kakissis interviewed President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Tuesday in Kyiv. Here's what he said about the importance of this satellite network that Ukraine is using.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)PRESIDENT VOLODYMYR ZELENSKYY: We need Starlink. We asked administration, government and SpaceX on different channels. We asked them to share with us Starlink only for military goals.MYRE: So the big issue has been this cooperation and intelligence sharing. Trump said back on Tuesday that intelligence sharing hadn't been cut, but what we saw yesterday did look like some sort of intentional action against Ukraine.INSKEEP: What options does Ukraine have if that kind of disruption continued?MYRE: I spoke with Mark Montgomery during this whole episode. He's a retired U.S. Navy rear admiral. He travels to Ukraine often to train and advise the military there. Now, he said Ukraine shouldn't go against Trump and attack Russian oil facilities, but he thinks there are still a number of things Ukraine could do. He suggested this approach.MARK MONTGOMERY: I'd turn to my military planners and say, good news, boys. I'm going to give you full operational planning to strike nonenergy targets in Russia. Have a field day. And you know what Vladimir Putin is going to find out? He's vulnerable everywhere, all the time, all at once.MYRE: Still, it's a difficult moment for Ukraine, which is taking hits on several fronts. Russia has stepped up attacks with ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones as Ukraine struggles with the lack of air defenses to counter these weapons, and Russia says openly that this is part of a broader campaign to take out Ukraine's electricity grid this winter, which looks to be the toughest one yet facing Ukraine.INSKEEP: NPR's Greg Myre. Thanks.MYRE: Sure thing, Steve.

sources.headline: UK's Streeting says he and Hegseth welcomed Starlink restoration in Ukraine
sources.text: WASHINGTON, Oct 15 - Britain's defense secretary said he and US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth welcomed the restoration of the Starlink service in Ukraine in talks on Thursday, but did not get into why the interruption happened.During an appearance on Fox News' "The Story with Martha MacCallum," Wes Streeting was asked, after his meeting with Hegseth, if the Pentagon restricted offensive and defensive capability for Ukraine in order to prevent strikes on Russian energy installations.He replied: "That's not my understanding. We didn't really get into why the service interruption had happened. We did reflect briefly on the fact that it had been restored and welcome that."Streeting said he was not going to speculate on why the interruption happened.Ukraine said Elon Musk’s SpaceX had restricted Starlink services on Wednesday, hampering the country's attack and air-defence drone missions.Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, which operates Starlink, said the US government controlled the system's speeds. REUTERS

Published: 5:29am, 15 Oct 2026Updated: 4:57pm, 15 Oct 2026

Tech billionaire Elon Musk called on Wednesday for Volodymyr Zelensky to “go” as Ukraine’s leader, after insisting any disruption to the war-torn country’s use of his satellite communications system was the fault of the US government, not his company.

The comments came as Kyiv raised doubts over US support for Ukraine in its war with Russia, accusing Washington this week of helping Moscow by failing to warn it of incoming missile strikes and hobbling Kyiv’s military response through changes to the SpaceX-designed system it uses for communications.

“And so the slaughter continues,” Musk wrote on X. “Time for Zelensky to go.”

Musk earlier said that “any limits on speed or usage” of his SpaceX company’s Starshield systems were “decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS”, referring to US President Donald Trump.

He drew a distinction between Starshield, which Ukraine relies on for battlefield communications, and the parallel Starlink civilian satellite system, which Kyiv also deploys but is not allowed to use for offensive operations.

Musk was responding to a post on X by Ukraine’s former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who said that “Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160km/h is being restored”, but that “removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defence”.

A Ukrainian serviceman prepares a Starlink system in 2024. Photo: Reuters

Ukrainian defence officials have suggested Washington is behind slower speeds reported on some internet terminals that help the country’s military hit Russian-occupied territory and operate interceptor drones.

Kyiv has also accused the United States of helping Russia by failing to warn it of incoming missile strikes, with the city hit by ballistic missiles for two nights in a row before air raid sirens could sound to warn residents to take cover.

A senior official in Kyiv also said that the United States had in recent days threatened to stop providing intelligence about Russian missile launches that Ukraine uses to thwart attacks – which Trump has denied.

Trump, facing key midterm elections next month in which soaring fuel prices are a major issue, has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for the squeeze on supplies and increase in prices at the pump.

Opposition Democrats in the US Senate and House denounced Trump’s administration over the reported interrupted connections.

“Trump’s making a choice – and it directly aids Putin’s slaughter of Ukrainian civilians,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrats said in a post on X, describing restrictions as “unconscionable” while Ukraine faced an onslaught of Russian drones and missiles.

In the Senate’s Foreign Relations Committee, top Democrat Jeanne Shaheen said the “restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starshield must stop immediately,” adding that “lives are at stake”.

Shaheen also said that the defence department is required to notify “Congress if it pauses or downgrades intelligence sharing with Ukraine”, and called on Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth to immediately provide that notification if there are changes.
